title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Imagine you are managing an investment fund. Your goal is simple: earn the highest possible return for your investors. However, you cannot invest however you like. Your fund has several rules: no single stock can account for more than 10% of the portfolio, and the maximum drawdown must remain below 30%. Maximum drawdown measures the largest cumulative decline in portfolio value from a previous peak to a subsequent low. It is one way of describing how much an investor could lose during a bad period.
There is another complication. In your estimates, investments with higher expected returns also tend to have greater downside risk. Putting everything into the investment with the highest expected return might therefore violate the fund’s risk limit.
This is a classic economic problem: how do we maximize an objective when some choices are not allowed? The method of Lagrange multipliers offers a systematic way to answer this question. It is useful not only in portfolio management but also in consumer choice, production planning, and resource allocation.

title: “Blog Post 1 for AEDS 6400” author: “Zhengyang Ding” output: html_document —
Suppose you are standing at the foot of a mountain, planning to climb to the top, and then return to the ground at the foot on the other side. Now imagine that there is a tunnel through the mountain, connecting your starting point and end point. Comparing the relative spatial location of the tunnel and your travel path with respect to the horizon, what do you find?
Through quick observation, you would discover that the tunnel lies completely beneath your travel route. In fact, you would realize that for any two points on or within the mountain, the straight line connecting them always lies inside the mountain. What does this phenomenon imply? What characteristics does the mountain’s landscape have?
The mountain, from a mathematical view, is a three-dimensional region. The property of this solid set that yields this phenomenon is convexity. A region is convex if the straight line segment connecting any two points within the region always lies inside the region. In two-dimensional space, a function is convex if its graph, within the range of any two points on it, lies below the straight line connecting the two points.
In mathematics, we define the convexity of a function as
\[
f\left(\lambda x_1 + (1-\lambda)x_2\right)
\leq
\lambda f(x_1) + (1-\lambda)f(x_2),
\qquad
\forall x_1,x_2\in\operatorname{dom}(f),\quad
\forall \lambda\in[0,1].
\]
There are several operations that preserve convexity, such as nonnegative weighted sums, composition with affine functions, and pointwise maximum. For example, if \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\) are convex functions and \(\alpha_i\geq0\), then the nonnegative weighted sum of the functions
\[
f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i f_i(x)
\]
is also convex.
To extend the use of convexity in solving mathematical problems, we expand the combination from two points to \(n\) points, then we get the definition of convex combination as follows:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i,
\qquad
\lambda_i\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i=1.
\]
This form of the weighted sum of variables with parameters reminds us of the definition of expectation. If the \(\lambda_i\)’s are interpreted as probabilities, then convex combinations could be interpreted by expected values. We therefore come to the following inequality named Jensen’s inequality:
\[
f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i\right)
\leq
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i f(x_i),
\]
or equivalently,
\[
f\left(\mathbb{E}[X]\right)
\leq
\mathbb{E}[f(X)].
\]
Following the definition of convex functions, we may also derive the convexity of sets. A set \(C\) is convex if, for any two points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) in \(C\),
\[
\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\in C,
\qquad
\forall\lambda\in[0,1].
\]
Moreover, the sublevel set of a convex function is also a convex set. For a convex function \(f\), its sublevel set at level \(\alpha\) is defined as
\[
C_{\alpha}
=
\left\{
x\in\operatorname{dom}(f)
\mid
f(x)\leq\alpha
\right\}.
\]
The convexity of feasible sets is particularly useful when we attempt to solve optimization problems (a feasible set for a series of constraints is the set of every point that satisfies all the constraints). When the feasible set is convex, together with appropriate properties with respect to the objective function, optimization problems often allow us to employ simplified calculation approaches and produce interior solutions.
Why should economists care about convexity and its connection with optimization? Convex preferences, feasible sets, and objective functions are closely related to whether optimization problems have well-behaved solutions and why local information could sometimes imply information on the global problem.

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Douban, a popular film and book review website from China, has a good reputation and a large audience who rate and comment on films and books from different countries and time periods. It is particularly known for its Top 250 film list, which ranks highly regarded films from around the world. The list is widely used by viewers looking for well-reviewed films. As a film fan, I have frequently referred to this list, along with individual ratings and reviews, when selecting films to watch.



The Webpage of Douban’s Top 250 Film List


The ranking of the list is calculated using an algorithm based on weighted ratings from different reviewers. The weighting system takes reviewers’ overall rating behavior into account, making the ranking different from the simple average rating that is directly displayed to users. This distinction raises an important question: once a film has entered the Top 250, does its visible average rating still provide useful information about its position within the list?
The question is especially relevant because the Top 250 already consists of highly rated films, so the range of visible ratings is relatively narrow. If average ratings are similar across different parts of the ranking, then a film’s visible rating may provide little additional information about how highly it is ranked. At the same time, ratings may differ systematically across genres and countries because audiences can have different preferences for different types of films.
Therefore, this blog answers two specific questions:
(1) Do visible average ratings vary systematically with a film’s position in the Top 250?
(2) Do average ratings differ systematically across film genres and countries?
Answering these questions can help us determine whether visible ratings are a useful tool for comparing films within the Top 250, or whether they should be interpreted in the context of a film’s characteristics.

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Data Analysis
In this blog, we employ RVEST using R to scrape data on the top 250 film list from the Douban website, attempting to answer these questions through some simple data analysis. We collect data on the ranking, country, year, and genre of each film within the Top 250 list, and again, employ R to conduct analysis and visualization.We group films respectively according to the ranking (50 films a group), production year (a decade for each group),the genre, and the country (we only analyze the major countries here). We then calculate and plot the average rating for each group.
We first discover that the average rating does not necessarily correlate with the ranking of a film. Indeed, we do not observe a downward trend of average ratings along with rankings (the invisible effective ratings follow this rule, as they are exactly the reference of the ranking!). Therefore, we may tell that the visible average ratings plays an insignificant part within this top list, as the effective rating is hardly correlated with the visible rating.



Average Rating by Ranking Group


We then check if different categories of films would exhibit different ratings. Different categories are not supposed to be assigned with different art values, therefore this might indicate some preferences of Chinese audience.
Regarding genre, we find that fantasy and mystery films receive particularly low scores, and crime films receive lower scores to some degree as well. It could be speculated that these are relatively niche genres, which possess relatively fewer audiences with strong preferences. Other genres generally receive high scores, with documentaries receiving the highest rating.



Average Rating by Genre Group


Moving to the category of country, because countries of production are relatively centralized for top films, we select some major countries for comparison, including China Hongkong, China Macao, China Taiwan, France, Britain, the U.S., Japan and South Korea. We find that Chinese audience seems to be critical on home country films compared with western major countries. A special finding is that Japan receives particularly low ratings, while South Korean films are highly recognized. This may also be explained by subjective tastes.



Average Rating by Country


Another attempt we made is to group years of production and see if there are any regularities. We find steady fluctuations by decades, without a strong direction of trend.



Average Rating by year

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Conclusion
In general, through the data we scraped from Douban’s top film list, we managed to conduct a series of statistical analysis. We find that the visible ratings among the top-listed films are of insignificant reference value, as they remain stable across rankings of the list. We also find that the Chinese audience might has preferences over documentaries and South Korean films, while domestic films, Japanese films, and films under the genre of mystery or fantasy receive generally less preferences.
The findings help us rationally and carefully treat the ratings on major review platforms. Our findings imply that visible ratings from the well-known Douban platform might lose effectiveness within the top 250 list, and ratings on films of certain types (Fantasy, Japanese, domestic, etc.) could be biased when cross-compared with other categories. It is possible that similar patterns exist among other similar rating platforms, which might be a path for future investigations.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Educational attainment is closely associated with labor market outcomes. People with higher levels of education may have better employment opportunities, higher earnings, and more stable labor market experiences. At the same time, these relationships may change over time as the broader economic environment changes.
This blog post explores the following question:
how are educational attainment and labor market outcomes related in the United States, and how does this relationship change over time?
The analysis focuses on U.S. adults aged 25-64 from 2000 to 2024. Individuals are divided into five groups according to educational attainment: less than high school, high school diploma, some college or an associate degree, four years of college or a bachelor’s degree, and five or more years of college or a graduate degree.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Educational attainment is closely associated with labor market outcomes. People with higher levels of education may have better employment opportunities, higher earnings, and more stable labor market experiences. At the same time, these relationships may change over time as the broader economic environment changes.
This blog post explores the following question:
how are educational attainment and labor market outcomes related in the United States, and how does this relationship change over time?
The analysis focuses on U.S. adults aged 25-64 from 2000 to 2024. Individuals are divided into five groups according to educational attainment: less than high school, high school diploma, some college or an associate degree, four years of college or a bachelor’s degree, and five or more years of college or a graduate degree.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Data and Mechanism
The data come from the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey (CPS). The analysis uses EDUC to measure educational attainment and WORKLY, INCWAGE, and WKSUNEM1 to measure different aspects of labor market outcomes. Individual-level ASEC sampling weights are used throughout the analysis.
Educational attainment is the main grouping variable. For each education group and year, we compare three outcomes: the share of individuals who worked during the year, median annual wage income, and the average number of weeks spent looking for work or on layoff. This descriptive approach allows us to examine how labor market outcomes differ across education groups and how these differences evolve over time.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Findings



Employment Experience Share by Educational Attainment


The first figure shows a clear and persistent positive relationship between educational attainment and employment. Individuals with higher levels of education are consistently more likely to have worked during the year. The gap between education groups remains substantial throughout the period: the employment rate is around 90% for individuals with five or more years of college, compared with roughly 60%-65% for those with less than a high school education.
The figure also suggests that employment outcomes are more volatile among less-educated groups. The decline around the 2008 financial crisis is particularly pronounced for individuals with less than a high school education, while the highest-education groups show relatively smaller changes over time.



Median Annual Wage by Educational Attainment


The second figure shows an even larger and persistent gap in earnings. Individuals with higher educational attainment consistently have higher median annual wage income. Throughout the period, the highest-education group has a median wage roughly three times that of the lowest-education group.
Although all education groups experience some fluctuations over time, the ranking across education groups remains remarkably stable. The gap in earnings therefore appears to be a persistent feature of the labor market rather than a pattern specific to a particular period.



Average Weeks Unemployed by Educational Attainment


The third figure measures the average number of weeks that individuals spent looking for work or on layoff during the year. During relatively stable periods, the education groups show distinct and fairly persistent levels: individuals with less education generally spend more weeks looking for work or on layoff, while those with higher education spend fewer weeks.
During major labor market disruptions, however, these differences become less distinct. Around the 2008 financial crisis and again around 2020 (where this trend is more salient), average weeks looking for work or on layoff increased across all education groups, and the lines of different groups show some overlap. Rather than maintaining the clear separation observed in stable periods, the education groups moved closer together as the overall labor market shock affected individuals across education levels. Once conditions became more stable, the groups again tended to separate into their usual relative levels.
This measure should be interpreted as the average number of weeks looking for work or on layoff among individuals for whom WKSUNEM1 is applicable. It does not measure the time required to find a job.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Conclusion
In general, our three sets of visual analyses reveal a consistent relationship between educational attainment and labor market outcomes in the United States from 2000 to 2024. Individuals with higher levels of education have a higher chance of working during the year, receive higher median wages, and are less likely to experience unemployment. These general trends persist over the observation window, and less-educated groups tend to experience larger fluctuations in employment. One should note that these findings are descriptive rather than causal, as other elements, such as work experience, occupation, and industry, may also contribute to the observed differences.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Buying a home today feels impossible for many Americans. But is this purely because houses are getting too expensive? Not necessarily. A booming housing market might be offset by rising incomes, and high price tags can sometimes be swallowed if borrowing costs are historically low.
This blog answers the following question: How has housing affordability in the United States changed over time, and what roles have house prices, mortgage rates, and household income played in this change?

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Buying a home today feels impossible for many Americans. But is this purely because houses are getting too expensive? Not necessarily. A booming housing market might be offset by rising incomes, and high price tags can sometimes be swallowed if borrowing costs are historically low.
This blog answers the following question: How has housing affordability in the United States changed over time, and what roles have house prices, mortgage rates, and household income played in this change?

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Data
The data source for this blog is the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis FRED database. We use its API to scrape data from the website.
Four FRED series are used:









Variable
FRED Series
Original Frequency
Role




Median sales price of new houses
MSPUS
Quarterly
Housing price


30-year fixed mortgage rate
MORTGAGE30US
Weekly
Borrowing cost


Real median household income
MEHOINUSA672N
Annual
Household purchasing power


Consumer Price Index
CPIAUCSL
Monthly
Inflation adjustment



The original data of different variables involve different frequencies, thus for the consistency within our analysis, the weekly mortgage rate and monthly CPI are transformed into quarterly averages. The quarterly median house price is kept at its original frequency. Annual median household income is matched to each quarter within the corresponding year.
For monetary values, the nominal median house price is converted into the real value to 2025 dollars using the CPI:
\[
RealHousePrice_t =
NominalHousePrice_t
\times
\frac{CPI_{2025}}{CPI_t}
\]
This adjustment allows house prices from different periods to be compared according to the same purchasing power.
Finally, I construct the house-price-to-income ratio:
\[
PriceIncomeRatio_t =
\frac{RealHousePrice_t}
{RealMedianHouseholdIncome_t}
\]
A higher value indicates that the price of ordinary houses is high relative to household’s average income, implying the average level of housing affordability.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Visualization Strategy
I use three time-series visualizations to analyze the trend on housing affordability. Each visualization focuses on a different component of housing affordability, and together they provide a broader picture of how the housing market has changed.



Figure 1: House Price Trend


The first visualization plots the median sales price of new houses in constant 2025 U.S. dollars. Looking at the real house prices, there is a long-run upward trend in general. Despite a few temporary downturns that might be correlated with macro economic recessions (like the 2008 financial crisis), the general trend goes up, and the level of real house prices is considerably higher in the 2020s than it was during the 1960s. The price approximately doubled over the past 60 years.



Figure 2: Mortgage Rate Trend


The house price alone doesn’t tell the whole story. The second visualization plots the quarterly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate. Mortgage rates represent the cost of financing a home purchase. At a same house price, a higher mortgage rate lowers the affordability.
The figure shows that the 30-year mortgage rate grew to approximately 18% in 1963-1980, then gradually declined for decades until 2020. The decline became particularly pronounced during the COVID-19 period, when mortgage rates reached a level of around 3%. After 2021, mortgage rates recovered significantly from the bottom level to around 7%.
This pattern implies that housing price alone cannot fully describe housing affordability during some period of times. During 1980-2020, the lowered cost of financing accompanied the rising real house price, keeping house affordability somewhat affordable. By contrast, the high house price in the 2020s combined an increase in mortgage rate created a worsened affordability environment.



Figure 3: Price-to-Income Ratio


The third visualization plots the ratio of real median house prices to real median household income, which directly compares the cost of housing with household income. Intense fluctuations are observed, with the cycle’s peak increasing each time.
The ratio was relatively stable around 4 in the mid-1980s and early 1990s. It then increased during the late 1990s and early 2000s, reaching 5 before the housing market crisis.
The ratio declined significantly when the financial crisis came in the late 2000s, which is consistent with the sharp decline in house prices shown in Figure 1.
After the financial crisis, the ratio recovered. During the 2010s, housing prices grew faster than household income, pushing the ratio upward, and then a setback came again in the late 2010s. The increase went sharp during 2020–2023, when the ratio approached 6.
The post-pandemic decline after 2022 is also clearly illustrated from the graph. The ratio falls substantially from its peak as real house prices declined. However, our graph 2 complements the explanation of regularity here, as mortgage rates increased substantially during the same period, which means that the cost of financing a home became considerably higher even though the price-to-income ratio declined. This comparison between Figures 2 and 3 indicates that the price-to-income ratio and mortgage rates capture different dimensions of affordability, which are both significant.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Conclusion
This project analyzes how housing affordability in the United States has changed over time by combining three dimensions of the housing market: real house prices, mortgage rates, and the house-price-to-income ratio.
The analysis shows that real house prices have increased significantly in the long run, despite several major downturns. At the same time, mortgage rates have experienced a long-term decline from the exceptionally high levels of the early 1980s, followed by a sharp increase after 2021.
The house-price-to-income ratio offers a trend of the relationship between housing costs and household resources. Its increase during the 2000s and especially the early 2020s suggests that housing became increasingly expensive relative to household income. The previous analysis on mortgage rate could help with the explanation to this trend.
The general takeaway of this study is that housing affordability relies on the interaction between housing price, household income, and borrowing cost. Taking early 2020s as an instance, the rapid house-price growth increased the price of housing relative to household income, while historically low mortgage rates temporarily reduced financing costs. After 2021, however, rising mortgage rates added another source of financial pressure for potential home buyers.
The visualization suggests that the economic burden of purchasing a house has increased over the long run, while this burden may have changed through different channels. Looking at house prices, income, and mortgage rates together offers a more informative picture of housing affordability than focusing on any single indicator.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Data and Method
To investigate this, I used historical data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED) through API access. I looked at three key variables: the median sales price of new houses, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, and the real median household income.
The observation window is 1963-2024, and variables are recorded on a seasonal basis (income data was coded only since 1980s). To ensure an apples-to-apples comparison over decades, I adjusted nominal house prices and incomes for inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
The analysis is conducted with three figures. The first and second firueres respectively use the variables of real housing price and 30-year mortgage rate. For the third graph, I calculate a price-to-income ratio that directly compares the cost of an average house to the average household’s purchasing power.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Takeaway
Method: I used Census FRED API data to analyze three core components of housing: inflation-adjusted house prices, 30-year mortgage rates, and the price-to-income ratio. They together offer an overview of the general housing affordability in the U.S. over the past decades.
Wage-Price Disconnect: Real house prices have surged over the long run, significantly outpacing household income growth and pushing the price-to-income ratio to historic highs.
The Rate Illusion: Historically low mortgage rates countered the severity of rising house prices in 1980-2020, temporarily keeping monthly payments somewhat affordable.
The Double Squeeze: The recent post-pandemic (after 2020) spike in mortgage rates, combined with already high housing prices, has fundamentally elevated the economic burden for potential home buyers.
Core Insight: Housing affordability is not just about the price tag; it relies heavily on the interaction between prices, income, and borrowing costs. Looking at any single indicator fails to capture the true financial burden on American households.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Is the American Dream geographically concentrated? As the national debate around inequality deepens, we explore the geographical distribution of people at different income levels. We look beyond national averages and zoom into the county level, which is the building blocks of local economies.
In this blog, we attempt to answer the following question: What is the geographical distribution of high- and low-income counties in the U.S., and is this spatial characteristic changing over time?

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Is the American Dream geographically concentrated? As the national debate around inequality deepens, we explore the geographical distribution of people at different income levels. We look beyond national averages and zoom into the county level, which is the building blocks of local economies.
In this blog, we attempt to answer the following question: What is the geographical distribution of high- and low-income counties in the U.S., and is this spatial characteristic changing over time?

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Data and Method
To conduct this analysis, we extract data county-level median household income from the U.S. Census Bureau through API, drawing on the American Community Survey (ACS). Because single-year ACS estimates only cover heavily populated areas, we used ACS 5-year estimates to ensure complete, reliable geographic coverage across the entire country. The latest round of statistics come from 2024, and we also extract statistics from a decade ago (2014) for comparative analysis.
Using R, we merge median household income data with geographic boundary shapefiles at the county level. To untangle genuine spatial shifts from the effects of inflation, we calculate each county’s relative income rank by assigning them to quintiles from the lowest 20% to the highest 20% nationally. In this way, we get to map the distributions of relative county-level income to the spatial map.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Analytical Findings
The Current Landscape: 2024



Figure 1: 2024 Relvative Income Distribution


The relative county-level income distribution map for 2024 reveals a clear geographic polarization. High-income counties (the top 20%) are not scattered randomly; they are tightly clustered along the Northeast Corridor, the West Coast tech hubs (like the Bay Area and Seattle), and a handful of booming inland metros (e.g., Denver, Austin, Nashville). Conversely, the lowest-income counties (bottom 20%) form a massive, contiguous block across the American South, stretching from the Appalachian Mountains down through the Mississippi Delta, alongside pockets of the Southwest.



Figure 2: 2024 Absolute Income Distribution


To validate this, the absolute median household income map (our median income data is directly used to map this) corroborates our findings. The spatial patterns align perfectly: the darkest, wealthiest counties (often exceeding 150,000 in median income) correspond to the coastal pink clusters, while the lowest brackets (frequently below 50,000) mirror the Southern red belt. This tells us that the relative ranking does reflect real wealth gaps between regions.
A Decade of Change: 2014 vs. 2024



Figure 3: 2014 Relvative Income Distribution


When we compare 2024 to a decade ago (2014), the general revelation is the stickiness of spatial inequality. The economic landscape of the wealthy coasts and the impoverished South remain remarkably unchanged.
Under the general revelation, a closer look reveals a hardening Matthew Effect (the rich get richer). Over the decade, certain suburban and exurban counties adjacent to major metropolitan hubs have shifted from middle-tier to top-tier categories. Meanwhile, many rural counties in the Midwest and South that were previously middle-income have slipped down the rankings. The map shows a subtle but significant consolidation of high-income status into fewer, more concentrated metro areas, while the areas left behind are sprawling.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Takeaway
Method: We extract Census ACS 5-year estimates and use R to map county-level relative income quintiles across the U.S. for both 2014 and 2024.
Spatial Polarization: The map reveals severe geographic clustering, with high-income counties concentrated on the coasts and low-income counties forming a massive, contiguous block across the South region.
Structural Stickiness: A decade-over-decade comparison shows strong persistence, as the broad geographic contours of wealth and poverty remain mainly unchanged.
Metropolitan Concentration: Over time, an emerging “Matthew Effect” is visible, with wealth further concentrating into core metropolitan hubs, while many rural counties slip down the relative rankings.
Core Insight: American income inequality fundamentally has spatial regularities, as economic opportunity and mobility remain tied to one’s zip code.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Analytical Findings - The Current Landscape: 2024



Figure 1: 2024 Relvative Income Distribution


The relative county-level income distribution map for 2024 reveals a clear geographic polarization. High-income counties (the top 20%) are not scattered randomly; they are tightly clustered along the Northeast Corridor, the West Coast tech hubs (like the Bay Area and Seattle), and a handful of booming inland metros (e.g., Denver, Austin, Nashville). Conversely, the lowest-income counties (bottom 20%) form a massive, contiguous block across the American South, stretching from the Appalachian Mountains down through the Mississippi Delta, alongside pockets of the Southwest.



Figure 2: 2024 Absolute Income Distribution


To validate this, the absolute median household income map (our median income data is directly used to map this) corroborates our findings. The spatial patterns align perfectly: the darkest, wealthiest counties (often exceeding 150,000 in median income) correspond to the coastal pink clusters, while the lowest brackets (frequently below 50,000) mirror the Southern red belt. This tells us that the relative ranking does reflect real wealth gaps between regions.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
section: Analytical Findings - A Decade of Change: 2014 versus 2024
text:
Analytical Findings - A Decade of Change: 2014 versus 2024



Figure 3: 2014 Relvative Income Distribution


When we compare 2024 to a decade ago (2014), the general revelation is the stickiness of spatial inequality. The economic landscape of the wealthy coasts and the impoverished South remain remarkably unchanged.
Under the general revelation, a closer look reveals a hardening Matthew Effect (the rich get richer). Over the decade, certain suburban and exurban counties adjacent to major metropolitan hubs have shifted from middle-tier to top-tier categories. Meanwhile, many rural counties in the Midwest and South that were previously middle-income have slipped down the rankings. The map shows a subtle but significant consolidation of high-income status into fewer, more concentrated metro areas, while the areas left behind are sprawling.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Imagine you are managing an investment fund. Your goal is simple: earn the highest possible return for your investors. However, you cannot invest however you like. Your fund has several rules: no single stock can account for more than 10% of the portfolio, and the maximum drawdown must remain below 30%. Maximum drawdown measures the largest cumulative decline in portfolio value from a previous peak to a subsequent low. It is one way of describing how much an investor could lose during a bad period.
There is another complication. In your estimates, investments with higher expected returns also tend to have greater downside risk. Putting everything into the investment with the highest expected return might therefore violate the fund’s risk limit.
This is a classic economic problem: how do we maximize an objective when some choices are not allowed? The method of Lagrange multipliers offers a systematic way to answer this question. It is useful not only in portfolio management but also in consumer choice, production planning, and resource allocation.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Turning the Problem into Mathematics
To understand the basic idea, let us simplify the fund’s investment choices into two categories. The first is a diversified equity portfolio, with an expected annual return of 12%. The second is a lower-risk asset portfolio, with an expected annual return of 4%. Let \(x\) and \(y\) represent the proportions invested in each category.
Because the fund must invest all its money,
\[
x+y=1.
\]
Its expected annual return, measured in percentage points, is
\[
R(x,y)=12x+4y.
\]
We also impose a simplified risk constraint:
\[
D(x)=8+44x\leq 30.
\]
Here, \(D(x)\) is an illustrative stress-risk score, expressed in percentage points. Its coefficients are hypothetical and are chosen only to demonstrate the method; it is not a forecast of actual maximum drawdown. The constraint implies that \(x\leq 0.5\).
Without a risk limit, the fund would put all its money into equities because their expected return is higher. With the limit, however, the most it can allocate to equities is 50%. The best feasible allocation is therefore \(x=0.5\) and \(y=0.5\), producing an expected return of 8%.
But how can we find this solution systematically, especially when there are many assets and constraints? This is where Lagrange multipliers become useful.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
The Logic of the Lagrangian
Instead of treating the objective and constraints as entirely separate problems, we combine them into one function:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}(x,y,\lambda,\mu)
={}&12x+4y\\
&+\lambda(1-x-y)\\
&+\mu\left[30-(8+44x)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term represents the return we want to maximize. The second incorporates the requirement that the entire portfolio be allocated. The third incorporates the risk limit. The new variables \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), called Lagrange multipliers, allow the optimization conditions to account for these restrictions.
The basic procedure is to find the point where the partial derivatives with respect to the decision variables are zero, while ensuring that the constraints are satisfied. For this example, the first-order conditions include
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y}=4-\lambda=0
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=12-\lambda-44\mu=0.
\]
These imply \(\lambda=4\) and \(\mu=8/44\approx 0.182\). Because the risk limit binds at the optimum, \(8+44x=30\), giving \(x=0.5\) and \(y=0.5\).
The important insight is that the multipliers are not arbitrary penalties selected by the fund manager. They are determined by the optimization conditions. In more general problems with inequality constraints, complementary slackness helps determine whether each constraint actually binds.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
section: What Does the Multiplier Tell Us?
text:
What Does the Multiplier Tell Us?
The multiplier \(\mu\) is the shadow price of the risk constraint. It measures how much the maximum expected return changes when the risk limit is relaxed by one unit, near the optimum.
Here, \(\mu=8/44\approx 0.182\). Raising the risk-score ceiling from 30 to 31 allows a larger equity allocation, increasing the model’s maximum expected annual return from 8.00% to about 8.18%. The multiplier therefore puts a number on the trade-off between accepting more risk and earning a higher return. This is a local result from our simplified model, not a guarantee about real investment performance.
In more complex problems, inequality constraints are handled using the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, which also identify whether a constraint is binding at the optimum.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
The Takeaway
Lagrange multipliers do more than provide a mathematical trick for solving constrained optimization problems. They offer a way to balance competing objectives while respecting real limitations. The central lesson is that the best decision is not necessarily the one with the highest possible return in isolation. It is the best decision among those that are feasible—and the multipliers help explain how much the constraints matter.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
References and Data Note
No empirical dataset is used in this example. All portfolio returns, risk-score coefficients, and investment constraints are illustrative assumptions.

Investor.gov: Introduction to Investing — background on asset allocation and diversification.
Goldberg and Mahmoud (2014), Drawdown: From Practice to Theory and Back Again — background on drawdown as a measure of investment risk.
Khan Academy: Interpretation of Lagrange Multipliers — the shadow-price interpretation.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Takeaways

Set the objective and constraints. Define what you want to maximize or minimize, then specify the limits that feasible choices must satisfy.
Build the Lagrangian. Combine the objective function and constraints using Lagrange multipliers, then use the first-order conditions and the constraints to find the optimum.
Interpret the multipliers. A multiplier on a binding constraint measures the marginal value of relaxing that constraint—the change in the best achievable objective from a small relaxation.
Use the result to make decisions. Multipliers show which constraints are costly and help evaluate whether relaxing a limit could improve the outcome.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Inter-generational income mobility studies the extent to which economic outcomes are associated across generations. To estimate this relationship, we first need to identify which children belong to which parents and then construct comparable measures of family income for each generation.
This project uses data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) and implements the parent-child matching procedure in Python with SQLite. The analysis has three main steps. First, the raw individual-level PSID data are reshaped into a longitudinal person-year dataset. Second, biological mothers and fathers are identified using the PSID parent-identification file and matched to their children with SQL. Finally, parent and child family income are constructed for both 2022 and the 2020–2022 period and used to estimate intergenerational income elasticity (IGE).
The main purpose of the SQL stage is to connect parent identifiers with longitudinal individual records, impose the required family restrictions, and aggregate income across parents and years.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Data and Matching Problem
The PSID provides information on individuals, families, and family relationships over time. The individual data used in this project contain observations for 2020 and 2022. Each individual is identified using a permanent person identifier constructed from the PSID family and person identifiers.
After processing the raw data, the longitudinal dataset contains variables such as:

person_id: permanent individual identifier
family_id: family identifier in the corresponding survey year
family_income: total income of the individual’s family unit
year: survey year
age: individual’s age

The parent-identification file provides the identifiers needed to connect a child to their biological mother and father. The relevant variables are PID2, PID3 for the child, PID4, PID5 for the biological mother, and PID23, PID24 for the biological father.
The first step is to convert these identifier components into the same person_id format used in the longitudinal individual data. This makes it possible to connect the parent-identification records directly to the individual-level observations.
The analysis constructs two income measures. The first uses family income observed in 2022. The second uses the average of family income observed in 2020 and 2022. In the final sample, both children and parents are restricted to ages 25–64 in 2022, and parent-child pairs are required to live in different families in the relevant year.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Loading the Data into SQLite
After the data-processing step, the two cleaned files are loaded into an SQLite database. The individual-level data are stored in an individual table, while the parent-identification data are stored in a separate parent_identification table.
import pandas as pd
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

project_root = Path(r"C:\Users\lenovo\PycharmProjects\6400_blog_6")
cleaned_dir = project_root / "data" / "cleaned_data"

individual_data = pd.read_csv(
    cleaned_dir / "individual_long.csv"
)

parent_identification = pd.read_csv(
    cleaned_dir / "parent_identification.csv"
)

conn = sqlite3.connect(
    cleaned_dir / "psid_matching.db"
)

individual_data[
    ["person_id", "family_id", "family_income", "year", "age"]
].to_sql(
    "individual",
    conn,
    if_exists="replace",
    index=False
)

parent_identification[
    ["child_id", "mother_id", "father_id"]
].to_sql(
    "parent_identification",
    conn,
    if_exists="replace",
    index=False
)
The two tables play different roles. The parent_identification table describes the family relationship, while the individual table contains the longitudinal information needed to measure income, family membership, and age.
Indexes are then created on the identifiers used repeatedly in the SQL joins.
cursor = conn.cursor()

cursor.execute("""
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_individual_person_year
ON individual(person_id, year)
""")

cursor.execute("""
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_parent_child
ON parent_identification(child_id)
""")

conn.commit()

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Constructing the Parent-Child Relationship
The parent-identification file contains separate identifiers for the biological mother and father. To make the subsequent SQL operations more straightforward, these two relationships are converted into a single parent-child bridge table.
cursor.execute("""
CREATE TABLE parent_child AS

SELECT
    child_id,
    mother_id AS parent_id,
    'mother' AS parent_type
FROM parent_identification
WHERE mother_id IS NOT NULL

UNION ALL

SELECT
    child_id,
    father_id AS parent_id,
    'father' AS parent_type
FROM parent_identification
WHERE father_id IS NOT NULL
""")

conn.commit()
The resulting table contains one row for each child-parent relationship. A child with both a biological mother and father can therefore appear twice, once for each parent.
This bridge table separates the relationship information from the longitudinal information. The parent_child table tells us who is connected to whom, while the individual table tells us what each person’s family income, family membership, and age were in a given year.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Matching Parents and Children in 2022
We first construct the single-year income measure using observations from 2022.
The SQL query joins the parent-child bridge table to the individual data twice: once to obtain the parent’s 2022 observation and once to obtain the child’s 2022 observation.
single_year_query = """
SELECT
    pc.child_id,

    AVG(parent.family_income)
        AS parent_income_2022,

    child.family_income
        AS child_income_2022,

    child.age
        AS child_age_2022,

    AVG(parent.age)
        AS parent_age_2022

FROM parent_child AS pc

JOIN individual AS parent
    ON pc.parent_id = parent.person_id
    AND parent.year = 2022

JOIN individual AS child
    ON pc.child_id = child.person_id
    AND child.year = 2022

WHERE parent.family_id != child.family_id

GROUP BY
    pc.child_id,
    child.family_income,
    child.age
"""

single_year = pd.read_sql_query(
    single_year_query,
    conn
)
The first JOIN retrieves the parent’s 2022 observation, while the second retrieves the child’s observation from the same longitudinal table. The condition
WHERE parent.family_id != child.family_id
requires the parent and child to belong to different families in 2022.
The query then uses GROUP BY to organize the matched observations by child. Since a child can be linked to both a biological mother and father, AVG(parent.family_income) combines the available parent income observations into a single parent-income measure. The same aggregation is used for parent age.
The resulting variables are therefore parent_income_2022, child_income_2022, child_age_2022, and parent_age_2022.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Constructing the 2020–2022 Income Measure
The second income measure uses information from both 2020 and 2022. Instead of relying on a single year’s income, we construct an average income measure across the two survey years.
The SQL query retrieves observations for both generations in both years:
multi_year_query = """
SELECT
    pc.child_id,

    AVG(parent_2020.family_income)
        AS parent_income_2020,

    AVG(parent_2022.family_income)
        AS parent_income_2022,

    child_2020.family_income
        AS child_income_2020,

    child_2022.family_income
        AS child_income_2022,

    child_2022.age
        AS child_age_2022,

    AVG(parent_2022.age)
        AS parent_age_2022

FROM parent_child AS pc

JOIN individual AS parent_2020
    ON pc.parent_id = parent_2020.person_id
    AND parent_2020.year = 2020

JOIN individual AS parent_2022
    ON pc.parent_id = parent_2022.person_id
    AND parent_2022.year = 2022

JOIN individual AS child_2020
    ON pc.child_id = child_2020.person_id
    AND child_2020.year = 2020

JOIN individual AS child_2022
    ON pc.child_id = child_2022.person_id
    AND child_2022.year = 2022

WHERE
    parent_2020.family_id != child_2020.family_id
    AND parent_2022.family_id != child_2022.family_id

GROUP BY
    pc.child_id,
    child_2020.family_income,
    child_2022.family_income,
    child_2022.age
"""

multi_year = pd.read_sql_query(
    multi_year_query,
    conn
)
Here, the parent and child observations are matched across both years. The family-separation condition is also imposed separately in 2020 and 2022, so the parent and child must belong to different families in both years.
After the SQL query returns the four income variables, Python constructs the two-year averages:
multi_year["parent_income_avg"] = (
    multi_year["parent_income_2020"]
    + multi_year["parent_income_2022"]
) / 2

multi_year["child_income_avg"] = (
    multi_year["child_income_2020"]
    + multi_year["child_income_2022"]
) / 2
The single-year and multi-year results are then merged using the child identifier:
matched_data = single_year.merge(
    multi_year,
    on="child_id",
    how="inner"
)
This produces a dataset in which the same matched children have both the 2022 income measures and the 2020–2022 average income measures.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Applying the Sample Restrictions
Before estimating the regressions, the analysis removes observations with non-positive income. This is necessary because the regression uses logarithmic income.
matched_data = matched_data[
    (matched_data["parent_income_2022"] > 0) &
    (matched_data["child_income_2022"] > 0) &
    (matched_data["parent_income_avg"] > 0) &
    (matched_data["child_income_avg"] > 0)
]
The working-age restriction is then applied using age in 2022:
matched_data = matched_data[
    matched_data["child_age_2022"].between(25, 64) &
    matched_data["parent_age_2022"].between(25, 64)
]
Thus, the final estimation sample contains parent-child pairs for which both generations are between 25 and 64 in 2022 and all income measures used in the regressions are positive.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Estimating Intergenerational Income Elasticity
The final step is to estimate the relationship between parent and child family income.
The analysis uses a log-log specification:
\[
\log(Y_i^{child})
=
\alpha
+
\beta\log(Y_i^{parent})
+
\varepsilon_i.
\]
The coefficient \[\beta\] is the intergenerational income elasticity (IGE). It measures how strongly differences in parent income are associated with differences in child income.
For the 2022 single-year measure, the analysis takes the natural logarithm of parent and child income and estimates the relationship using OLS:
single_year["log_parent_income"] = np.log(
    single_year["parent_income_2022"]
)

single_year["log_child_income"] = np.log(
    single_year["child_income_2022"]
)

X = sm.add_constant(
    single_year["log_parent_income"]
)

model_single = sm.OLS(
    single_year["log_child_income"],
    X
).fit()
The same procedure is applied to the 2020–2022 average income:
multi_year["log_parent_income"] = np.log(
    multi_year["parent_income_avg"]
)

multi_year["log_child_income"] = np.log(
    multi_year["child_income_avg"]
)

X = sm.add_constant(
    multi_year["log_parent_income"]
)

model_multi = sm.OLS(
    multi_year["log_child_income"],
    X
).fit()
The analysis extracts the estimated IGE coefficient, standard error, p-value, sample size, and R-squared from each model and saves them to the regression results file.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Results
The two specifications produce the following results:



Income measure
Observations
IGE
Standard Error
R-squared




2022 single-year income
1,635

0.065


2020–2022 average income
1,635

For the 2022 single-year measure, the estimated IGE is 0.245 with a standard error of 0.023. For the 2020–2022 average measure, the estimated IGE increases to 0.280, with a standard error of 0.022.
The results indicate a positive relationship between parent and child family income in both specifications. The higher IGE obtained using the two-year average also suggests that the estimated intergenerational income relationship is sensitive to how income is measured over time.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Life-Cycle Bias
Income is not necessarily a stable measure of an individual’s long-run economic position. A person’s income in any particular year can contain temporary fluctuations. Using only one year’s income may therefore introduce measurement noise into the intergenerational income relationship.
The single-year specification uses family income observed in 2022:
\[
\log(Y_i^{child,2022})
=
\alpha
+
\beta\log(Y_i^{parent,2022})
+
\varepsilon_i.
\]
The alternative specification uses average family income over 2020 and 2022:
\[
\log\left(
\frac{Y_i^{child,2020}+Y_i^{child,2022}}{2}
\right)
=
\alpha
+
\beta
\log\left(
\frac{Y_i^{parent,2020}+Y_i^{parent,2022}}{2}
\right)
+
\varepsilon_i.
\]
Averaging income across multiple years can reduce the influence of temporary income fluctuations and provide a measure that is closer to an individual’s longer-run economic position.
In our results, the estimated IGE increases from 0.245 using 2022 income to 0.280 using the 2020–2022 average. The R-squared also increases from 0.065 to 0.092. This comparison illustrates how the estimated degree of intergenerational persistence can change when income is measured over a longer period.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
The Takeaway
This project demonstrates how SQL can be used to solve a longitudinal parent-child matching problem using PSID data.
The main steps are:

Reshape the PSID data into a person-year structure so individuals can be tracked across 2020 and 2022.
Construct a parent-child bridge table from the biological parent identifiers.
Use SQL JOIN operations to connect parents and children to their individual-level observations.
Use GROUP BY and aggregation to construct parent-level income and age measures.
Construct both single-year and multi-year income measures to examine the sensitivity of IGE to income measurement.
Estimate log-log OLS regressions to obtain the intergenerational income elasticity.

The main lesson is that SQL provides a clear way to organize relationship matching, longitudinal joins, and aggregation when working with complex panel data. In this project, the parent-child bridge table connects the family relationship information to the longitudinal PSID records, while the SQL joins and aggregation operations transform those matched records into the income measures required for the final IGE analysis.

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Takeaways
Visible ratings add limited information within the Top 250. Average ratings show little relationship with ranking, so small rating differences should not be over-interpreted.
Ratings differ across genres and countries. Fantasy, mystery, and Japanese films receive relatively lower ratings, while documentaries and South Korean films receive higher ratings, suggesting differences in audience preferences.
Use ratings as a reference, not a final decision rule. When choosing a film, viewers should consider ranking, genre, country, and personal preferences together rather than relying only on the visible rating.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Takeaways

Higher education is consistently associated with better labor market outcomes. More-educated individuals are more likely to have worked during the year and have substantially higher median wages.
The education gap extends beyond employment and earnings. Less-educated individuals generally spend more weeks looking for work or on layoff, suggesting less favorable labor market experiences.
Economic downturns affect all education groups. The 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 shock are visible across the figures, with labor market outcomes changing substantially across all education groups.
Crisis periods temporarily reduce the differences across education groups. During major labor market disruptions, average weeks looking for work or on layoff rise across education groups and the lines show substantial overlap. In more stable periods, the groups tend to separate into clearer and more distinct levels.
These findings are descriptive rather than causal. The observed differences may also reflect other factors, such as work experience, occupation, industry, and demographic characteristics. Therefore, the analysis documents the relationship between education and labor market outcomes rather than identifying a causal effect of education.

title: Urbanization and Economic Development: An Interactive View
text:
Urbanization is an important part of economic development. As countries become richer, economic activity and population often become increasingly concentrated in urban areas. However, countries do not necessarily experience this process in the same way. Some countries combine relatively high incomes with very high levels of urbanization, while others remain highly urbanized despite having much lower income levels.
This blog post explores the following question:
how are countries’ levels of urbanization related to real GDP per capita, and how do countries follow different development paths over time?
The analysis covers countries and economies from 2000 to 2024. By combining real GDP per capita with the share of the population living in urban areas, the visualization allows us to examine both differences across countries and changes within countries over time.

title: Urbanization and Economic Development: An Interactive View
text:
Urbanization is an important part of economic development. As countries become richer, economic activity and population often become increasingly concentrated in urban areas. However, countries do not necessarily experience this process in the same way. Some countries combine relatively high incomes with very high levels of urbanization, while others remain highly urbanized despite having much lower income levels.
This blog post explores the following question:
how are countries’ levels of urbanization related to real GDP per capita, and how do countries follow different development paths over time?
The analysis covers countries and economies from 2000 to 2024. By combining real GDP per capita with the share of the population living in urban areas, the visualization allows us to examine both differences across countries and changes within countries over time.

title: Urbanization and Economic Development: An Interactive View
text:
Data and Mechanism
The data come from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. The analysis uses NY.GDP.PCAP.KD to measure real GDP per capita and SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS to measure urban population as a percentage of total population. The data cover the period from 2000 to 2024 and are classified by continent.
Real GDP per capita is the main variable on the horizontal axis, while urban population is shown on the vertical axis. Because GDP per capita varies substantially across countries, it is displayed on a logarithmic scale. Each point represents a country in a particular year, and colors identify continents.
The visualization is interactive rather than static. A year slider and animation allow readers to follow countries from 2000 to 2024, while continent colors facilitate group comparisons. Hovering over individual observations provides the country name and the corresponding values of real GDP per capita and urban population. These features allow the reader to examine both the overall cross-country pattern and the different paths taken by individual countries.

title: Urbanization and Economic Development: An Interactive View
text:
Findings


The visualization shows a broad tendency for higher-income countries to have higher levels of urbanization. Countries toward the right side of the graph are generally more urbanized than countries at lower income levels.
However, the points do not form a single tight pattern. Countries with similar levels of real GDP per capita can have substantially different urban population shares. This suggests that countries can reach similar income levels while having very different patterns of population settlement.
There are also clear differences across continents. European countries are generally concentrated in the higher-income and highly urbanized part of the graph. Many African countries appear at lower income levels and lower or intermediate levels of urbanization, although there is considerable variation within the continent.
Asian countries span a particularly wide range, including low-income and less-urbanized countries as well as high-income and highly urbanized economies. The Americas and Oceania also include countries with relatively high urbanization despite not being among the highest-income economies.
The time animation reveals another important pattern. From 2000 to 2024, many countries move both upward and to the right, indicating increases in urbanization and real GDP per capita. African and European countries move at a mild pace, remaining their relative positions unchanged, as they remain at two different sides of the graph. Meanwhile, Asian countries move in a more aggressive way, as shifts are drastic across time for some countries, and while some countries went further urbanized, some went in the opposite direction.
Some countries exhibit strong development performance and urbanization during our observation window. China provides a particularly visible example. Its urban population share increased from about 36% in 2000 to about 66% in 2024, while its real GDP per capita also increased substantially. Türkiye and Thailand show similarly pronounced movements toward higher urbanization and income.
The interactive features therefore add substantive information beyond a static scatterplot. The year slider and animation allow readers to observe changes over time, the continent colors make geographic differences easier to compare, and the hover information allows individual countries to be identified and examined. Readers can move from the overall pattern to specific countries and back again without needing separate figures for different years or groups.

title: Urbanization and Economic Development: An Interactive View
text:
Takeaways

Higher-income countries tend to be more urbanized. The visualization shows a broad positive relationship between real GDP per capita and the urban population share, but the relationship is far from uniform.
Countries at similar income levels can have very different urbanization rates. Geographic and country-specific differences are an important part of the overall pattern.
Urbanization and income often increase together over time. Many countries move upward and to the right between 2000 and 2024, but the magnitude of these changes varies substantially across countries.
Countries follow different development paths. The animation reveals large differences in the speed and direction of changes in urbanization, including countries that show little change or even declines in their urban population share.
Interactivity adds substantive value to the analysis. The ability to move through time, compare continents, and identify individual countries reveals patterns that would be difficult to communicate clearly in a single static graph.

Overall, the visualization suggests that there is no single path from economic development to urbanization. Instead, countries share a broad pattern of higher income and greater urbanization while following substantially different trajectories over time.
